arr.title: Annual recurring revenue
arr.content:
ARR is the annualised value of active subscriptions at period end -- the run-rate, not the period's revenue.

For Fair Isaac Corporation: this is Software/Platform ARR only -- it excludes the Scores segment's royalty-per-pull revenue entirely. ARR growth leads reported Software revenue growth by roughly a year.

What to watch:

  • Net new ARR per period
  • ARR growth versus Software segment revenue growth

arrMix.title: ARR mix: Platform vs non-platform
arrMix.content:
FICO's Software ARR splits between the modern, cloud-native FICO Platform and non-platform (legacy on-premise decisioning and professional-services) ARR.

For Fair Isaac Corporation: Platform revenue grew 84% YoY in Q4 FY2026 while non-platform fell 12% YoY, and Platform ARR has now overtaken non-platform ARR -- the mix shift is the thesis for the Software segment, separate from the Scores regulatory risk.

What to watch:

  • Whether Platform's net new ARR outpaces non-platform's decline (migration adding value, not just moving it)
  • Pace of the crossover continuing versus stalling

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Fair Isaac Corporation: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Fair Isaac Corporation: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Fair Isaac Corporation: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Fair Isaac Corporation: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Fair Isaac Corporation: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Fair Isaac Corporation: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

nrr.title: Net revenue retention
nrr.content:
NRR is revenue from a cohort of customers a year later, including expansion and churn, as a percentage of the starting revenue. This is the blended Software/Platform figure.

For Fair Isaac Corporation: above 100% means the existing base grows on its own; best-in-class SaaS runs 110-130%. This metric has no bearing on the Scores segment, which is priced per score pulled rather than subscribed.

What to watch:

  • NRR trend
  • Gross retention if disclosed

nrrMix.title: Net revenue retention: Platform vs non-platform
nrrMix.content:
Net revenue retention measured separately for the Platform and non-platform halves of the Software ARR base.

For Fair Isaac Corporation: Platform NRR running well above non-platform NRR confirms the migration is expansionary for customers who move, not just a relabeling of the same spend.

What to watch:

  • Non-platform NRR falling toward 100% or below as the legacy base shrinks and churns
  • Platform NRR holding above 110% as it scales

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Fair Isaac Corporation: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Fair Isaac Corporation: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Fair Isaac Corporation: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

segmentRevenue.title: Segment revenue: Scores vs Software
segmentRevenue.content:
FICO reports two segments: Scores (royalty-like fees each time a FICO Score is pulled, mostly mortgage, auto and credit-card B2B plus myFICO B2C) and Software (analytics/decision-management, increasingly sold as Platform SaaS).

For Fair Isaac Corporation: Scores carries FICO's highest margins and funded the buyback for years, but is the segment under direct regulatory attack -- FHFA has opened conforming-mortgage scoring to VantageScore 4.0 and FHA follows from January 2027. Software is the segment management is betting the future on.

What to watch:

  • Scores revenue growth decelerating as VantageScore wins mortgage volume and 2027 pricing is frozen under the Preferred Program
  • Software overtaking Scores as the larger segment

segmentOperatingIncome.title: Segment operating income: Scores vs Software
segmentOperatingIncome.content:
Operating income by segment, before corporate overhead.

For Fair Isaac Corporation: Scores has historically carried far higher margins than Software, so a shift in the revenue mix toward Software is not automatically margin-accretive even while it is growth-accretive -- watch whether Software's margin is converging toward Scores' as Platform scales.

What to watch:

  • Software segment margin trend as Platform ARR scales past the cost of migrating customers off legacy software
  • Scores segment margin under pressure from the $65m antitrust settlement accrual and competitive pricing responses to VantageScore

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Fair Isaac Corporation: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
